description: Ember Trace is a two-person geospatial AI team from Brazil. Isabella Subtil Norberto (PhD candidate, UNESP; Visiting Researcher, FGI) works on AI and photogrammetry, building 3D multispectral point clouds from LiDAR. Clodoaldo Júnior (PhD candidate, ITA; ex-geospatial data scientist) works on AI and remote sensing, using deep learning for satellite positioning. Together we test whether trends in Brazil’s fire-season climate and fires are real or just noise.
summary: Ember Trace team investigates whether Brazil's hotter, drier fire-season climate explains its fires. Using NASA GPM IMERG rainfall, GLDAS soil moisture, MERRA-2 temperature and vapor pressure deficit (VPD), NASA FIRMS (MODIS/Aqua) active fires, and NOAA CPC station temperature, we analyzed 24 years (2001–2024) of August–October trends in the Amazon, Cerrado and Pantanal. We first showed that the classic Mann-Kendall trend test flags 47% of trend-free, persistent series, so we used a test against an autocorrelated (AR(1)) null with false-discovery-rate control, which cuts that to 8.6%. The Cerrado warms about 0.5 °C per decade in station data (up to 1.0 °C in reanalyses), dries and has higher VPD, robustly across three temperature sources and five time windows. Yet Cerrado fire counts fall 18% per decade. After removing trends, year-to-year fire counts still track VPD (ρ = +0.73) and rain (ρ = −0.63): climate explains which years burn more, not the long-term trend. Everything is open and reproducible in Colab notebooks.
details:
What it does. Ember Trace team is a trend-detective analysis of the climate drivers of fire in Brazil. For three biomes (Amazon, Cerrado, Pantanal) it measures how fire-season (August–October) rainfall, soil moisture, vapor pressure deficit (VPD) and temperature changed from 2001 to 2024, how fire detections changed from 2002 to 2024, and whether the two are connected.

Figure 1. Red marks changes that favor fire. Dots show where the trend is statistically reliable (after false-discovery control).

How it works.

  1. Monthly NASA data (GPM IMERG precipitation, GLDAS soil moisture and air temperature, MERRA-2 temperature and humidity, from which we derive VPD) are put on one 0.25° grid over Brazil and aggregated to one value per year for the fire season.
  2. NOAA CPC station-based temperature is added as an independent check on the two model-based temperature products.
  3. Trends are estimated with the Sen slope. Significance uses a Mann-Kendall test against an autocorrelated AR(1) null, with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate control for maps. Abrupt shifts are located with the Pettitt test.
  4. NASA FIRMS MODIS active fires (Aqua satellite only) are counted per biome and compared with climate using Spearman correlations after removing each series' own trend.

Why it is rigorous. With only 24 yearly points, the classic Mann-Kendall test flags 47% of persistent but trend-free series as "trending". We measured this with 10,000 simulated series per autocorrelation level and built the analysis around a test that lowers that rate to 8.6% (with FDR). We then checked every key result against three temperature sources and five time windows, and we report where the results fail (the Pantanal temperature trend depends on the time window).

What we found. The Cerrado warms about 0.5 °C per decade in station data (up to 1.0 °C per decade in reanalyses), dries (soil moisture −7% per decade) and has higher VPD (+0.23 kPa per decade). Temperature trends are significant in 15 of 15 source-by-window combinations, and a step around 2014 appears in all three temperature sources. Cerrado fire counts nevertheless fall by 18% per decade. After removing trends, year-to-year fire counts in the Cerrado correlate with VPD (ρ = +0.73) and rain (ρ = −0.63). Climate therefore explains which years burn more, not the long-term decline in counts.

Figure 2. Cerrado fire counts fall 18% per decade, yet the hotter, drier years still burn more.

Benefits and intended impact. The result warns against reading falling fire counts as falling climate pressure, and suggests monitoring VPD and soil moisture to anticipate severe fire seasons. This is an implication of the correlations, not a tested forecast. The method is a template for any short, persistent Earth-observation time series. All code, tables and figures are open.

Tools. Python in Google Colab: xarray, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, matplotlib, geopandas, regionmask, geobr, statsmodels, pymannkendall, earthaccess. Data: NASA GES DISC (GPM IMERG, GLDAS, MERRA-2), NASA FIRMS, NOAA PSL CPC, IBGE biome boundaries.

What is creative. The "case file" framing (the suspect is the trend test itself), the sanity test that quantifies false alarms before any result is reported, the use of an independent station-based source as arbiter between two models, and publication-quality figures with colorblind-safe palettes where red always means "change that favors fire".

Factors we considered and limits. Autocorrelation, multiple testing across 25,600 pixels, grid mismatch between products (0.1° to 0.5°), VPD derived from monthly means, Aqua orbit drift after about 2022, active fire versus burned area, and the fact that correlation is not causation (ENSO, deforestation, land use and fire management are not modeled).
